title: Evelyn and the TimeBand: The Golden Gate Bridge
notes: Mission 3. Choices with 'route' go to the first matching target by state (side-quest payoffs).

s01.title: The Third Mission
paragraphs: Knock, knock! It is Dr. Ada Finch. She has the TimeBand in her case.
"Evelyn, I need you again," she says. She holds up a picture of a big orange bridge. "This is the Golden Gate Bridge. It is in San Francisco."

"On May 27, 1937, the new bridge opened. No cars came that day. Only people! They walked across. It was called Pedestrian Day. Pedestrian means a person who walks. The museum has old films. But no one recorded the sounds up close. Can you?"
You grin. Three green dots light up on the band.
"Same rules," says Dr. Finch. "Each trip uses one dot. Coming home is free. Watch, and be kind, but don't change what happened. To record, press the red button and hold still."
"And one more thing," she says. "In 1937, kids dressed a little different."

s02.title: Clothes from 1937
paragraphs: Dr. Finch opens the case. Inside is a blue dress with a white collar. There is a yellow sweater, white socks, and brown shoes with a strap.
You put them on. You spin. The dress spins too.
Mom laughs. "You look like a girl from long ago," she says. "Yellow, like a sunflower."
Mom keeps bees. She holds up a piece of honeycomb. "Bees build with wax," she says. "Each little room has six sides. That shape is strong, and it does not use much wax."
"Bridge builders think like bees," says Dr. Finch. "Strong, but not too heavy."

s04.title: A Bridge on the Table
paragraphs: Dr. Finch stacks two piles of books. "These are the towers," she says.
She ties a string to a chair. She lays it over the books. She ties the other end to a chair, too. The string sags in the middle, like a smile.
Then she hangs a paper road from the string with little threads.
"This is a suspension bridge," she says. "Suspend means hang. The road hangs from the cables."
You press on the road. The string pulls tight. The books press down on the table.
"The cables pull," says Dr. Finch. "The towers push. That is how it holds up."

s03.title: The Mission Map
s03.place: The TimeBand screen, in your kitchen
paragraphs: You tap the band. A map pops up. It shows blue water between two hills.
"This water is the Golden Gate," says Dr. Finch. "Ships sail in and out here. For a long time, there was no bridge. People rode boats across."
Four dots blink on the map.
1933. A ferry boat, before the bridge.
1936. Workers making the big cables.
May 27, 1937. Pedestrian Day! Picking a place is free.
May 28, 1937. The day after.
"What you learn on one trip can help on another," says Dr. Finch. "But you only have three dots."

s05.title: The Ferry Boat
s05.place: On a ferry boat on the bay, 1933
paragraphs: Zap! You are on a big white boat. The deck hums under your shoes.
Cars are parked inside the boat, in rows. Their owners stand by them. "There is no bridge yet," a man says. "So the cars ride the ferry."
You look out the window. There is the Golden Gate. It is just water and hills. No bridge at all.
"Some days, cars wait in a line for hours," the man says.
The band shows a clock. You have one hour.
Then a cold, gray cloud rolls over the water. It is fog!

s06.title: Into the Fog
paragraphs: Outside, the air is wet and cold. You can't see the hills. You can't see the water.
"Fog is a cloud that sits low, on the water," says a sailor. "Wet air blows over the cold sea. It cools down and makes fog."
Then you hear it. BOOOOO! The sound is so deep, your tummy shakes.
"That's a foghorn," says the sailor. "When ships can't see, they listen. The horn tells them where the land is."
You count. BOOOOO. Then quiet. Then BOOOOO again. Now it's not scary. It is a helper.

s07.title: The Big Plan
paragraphs: The sailor shows you a newspaper. It has a drawing of a bridge.
"A man named Joseph Strauss is in charge," he says. "He has wanted to build this bridge for years. Work just began."
"And Irving Morrow is the architect," he says. "He draws how it will look."
The band crackles. It is Dr. Finch! "Lots of people helped," she says. "A quiet man named Charles Ellis did much of the hard math. For a long time, hardly anyone knew."
"Some people say it can't be built," the sailor says. "The water is deep. The wind is strong. And look at this fog!"
You smile. You know a secret. They will build it.

s08.title: The Spinning Wheels
paragraphs: Zap! You are on a windy hill. Below you, the two orange towers stand in the water. But there is no road yet!
Long wires run from the hill, up over the towers, and down to the other side.
A wheel zips along the wires, way up high. It carries a wire across. Then another wheel comes back.
"They call it spinning," says a worker by you. "Back and forth, back and forth, all day."
High up, there is a skinny walkway made of wire and wood. Workers walk on it.

s09.title: Sam and His Hard Hat
paragraphs: The worker smiles. "I'm Sam," he says. He knocks on his hat. Knock, knock! It is hard, like a shell.
"This is a hard hat," says Sam. "Mr. Strauss says we all must wear one. If a tool falls from up high, the hat keeps my head safe."
He puts a spare one on your head. It is too big. It slips over your eyes! You both laugh.
"Not many jobs had hats like this before," says Sam. "Now we do."

s10.title: Thousands of Wires
s10.place: Where the cable comes down to the ground, 1936
paragraphs: Sam shows you a wire. It is thin, a little thinner than a pencil.
"One wire can't hold a bridge," says Sam. "But we put thousands of them side by side. Over twenty-seven thousand wires, in one cable!"
A big machine hugs the wires. It squeezes them into one round cable. It is so thick, you could not wrap your arms around it.
"Lots of thin wires make one strong cable," Sam says. "Like lots of hairs make one strong braid."
You think of your curls. Ha!

s11.title: The Safety Net
paragraphs: The band shows you a view under the bridge. There is a big rope net. It hangs under the workers, the whole way across.
"Mr. Strauss put that net there," says Sam. "If a worker falls, the net catches him."
"Did it ever catch someone?" you ask.
"Yes!" says Sam. "It caught some of my friends. They started a club. Its name means they fell only halfway down, and the net saved them."
You look at the net. It is like a giant hammock.

s12.title: Orange Paint
paragraphs: Painters are at work on the steel. Their brushes go swish, swish.
"Why orange?" you ask.
"The steel came here painted red-orange, to stop rust," says Sam. "Mr. Morrow, the architect, saw it. He liked it! So he picked a color like it. It's called International Orange."
"Orange looks nice with the hills and the sky. And you can see it in the fog," Sam says. "That helps ships and planes."
"The Navy wanted black and yellow stripes," he says. "Like a bee!"
You giggle. Mom would like that. But orange is better.

s14.title: Waiting at the Gate
s14.place: The gate on the city side, 5:50 a.m., May 27, 1937
paragraphs: Zap! It is early. The sky is gray with fog. And there are people everywhere!
Moms, dads, and kids. Big kids from school. A man with a tuba. Two girls with roller skates. It is a huge crowd.
"Thousands of people are here," says a lady. "We all want to be first!"
Each person pays a quarter to walk on the bridge.
A little girl in a red dress holds a puppy. She waves at you. "I'm Dottie! This is Peanut!" Peanut licks your hand. It tickles.
The crowd pushes and wiggles. The gate is still shut.

s15.title: Six O'Clock!
paragraphs: It is six o'clock. BOOOOO! BOOOOO! The foghorns blast, loud and deep. The sound rolls over the fog and the water.
Clank! The gates open. The crowd cheers. People run, walk, and skip onto the new orange bridge.
This is it! This is the sound the museum wants. You lift the band. Your finger is on the red button.
The horns blast again. BOOOOO!

s16.title: Onto the Bridge
paragraphs: You walk out onto the bridge. It is so wide! It is wide enough for six cars. But today, there are no cars. Just feet.
Tap, tap, tap. Thousands of feet. Clip, clop. Shoes on the road.
You look over the side. Way, way down is the water. The road is very high up. A ship looks like a toy.
The two orange towers rise into the fog. Cables sweep from tower to tower, like a long jump rope at rest.
Dottie holds your hand. Peanut trots along.
"My dad helped build this bridge," says Dottie. "He's here somewhere."

A boy runs past. "I'm racing to the other side!" he yells.
Everybody wants to be the first to do something. First to skate. First on stilts. First to play a tuba!

paragraphs: Now the tower is right next to you. You tip your head back. Way, way back. It goes up into the fog!
The tower is orange. It has steps near the top, where it gets thinner, like a wedding cake. It has long lines that run up and down. That makes it look even taller.
The band crackles. It is Dr. Finch! "Today, we call that style Art Deco," she says. "Irving Morrow, the architect, drew it that way."
You put your hand on the steel. It is cold. The tower pushes down, deep under the water. The cables pull on it from up high.

paragraphs: "Don't worry, Dottie. I'll help," you say.
You look under a bench. No Peanut. You look by the hot dog stand. Just a dropped bun.
The crowd is tall. You are small. It's hard to see over all the coats and hats.
The rail is right there. If you stood on it, you could see far. But the water is a long way down.
Or you could stop, close your eyes, and listen. Puppies make noise.

s21.title: Found Him!
paragraphs: You close your eyes. You hear feet. You hear the wind. You hear a tuba.
Then you hear it. Yip! Yip, yip!
You open your eyes. Peanut is by the man on stilts! He is chewing a bun.
You scoop him up. You run back. "Peanut!" yells Dottie. She hugs him, and he licks her nose.
Dottie gives you a paper sunflower from her pocket. "For you," she says. "So I can always find you in a crowd."
A tall man runs up. He has a cap and a big smile. "Thank you!" he says. "I'm Dottie's dad. I'm Gus."

s22.title: Gus's Story
s22.place: On the bridge with Dottie's family
paragraphs: "I helped build this bridge," says Gus. "I worked way up high, on the cables."
"I wore a hard hat every day," he says. "And under us was a big net, in case we fell."
He pats the rail. "I'm proud of it. Lots of us worked hard. And now everybody gets to walk on it."
Dottie holds Peanut tight. "Come to the middle with us, Evelyn!"
This would be a good story to record. Or you could go to the middle, where the two crowds meet.

The road under your feet moves, just a tiny bit. You feel it in your shoes.
"Is it falling?" asks a boy.
"No," says a man in a hard hat. "It is made to sway in the wind. If it was stiff, the wind could hurt it. It bends a little, so it does not break."
You think of a tall tree. It bends in the wind, but it stays up.

You look up. The bridge goes right over the fort! A big steel arch jumps over it, like a rainbow.
"They planned to tear the fort down," says a soldier. "But Mr. Strauss said no. He made the bridge jump over it instead."
But you can hardly see the bridge. The fog is so thick. It is gray, gray, gray.

So you wait. You listen. BOOOOO! Far up high, the foghorns blast. It is six o'clock! The gates are open.
Then the wind blows. The fog starts to slide away, like a blanket pulled off a bed.
First you see the orange tower. Then the big cables. Then the road, with tiny people walking on it!
The sun comes out. The bridge glows orange.

s30.title: Mr. Strauss
paragraphs: A short man in a dark suit steps up. It is Joseph Strauss.
He does not give a long speech. He reads a poem. He wrote it about the bridge.
"At last the mighty task is done," he reads. "Its towers pierce the sky."
People clap. You look at the orange towers. Then you think of the workers, the net, and the thousands of wires. It was a mighty task. Lots of people did it together.
Your finger is on the red button.

g_foghorns.title: The Six O'Clock Horns
paragraphs: You are not scared. You know what a foghorn is for. It helps ships find their way.
So you hold still. Very still. BOOOOO! BOOOOO! Then the clank of the gates, and a huge cheer.
Beep, beep! Recording saved. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch plays it. The kitchen fills with the deep horns of 1937. Mom covers her ears and laughs.
"Evelyn," says Dr. Finch, "that is the start of Pedestrian Day!"

g_cable.title: What's Inside
paragraphs: "It's not one big piece," you say. "It's lots and lots of thin wires. Over twenty-seven thousand! A machine squeezed them tight."
"Like a braid," says a girl.
"Yes!" you say. "Lots of thin wires make one strong cable."
The kids pat the cable. You hold still and record them all saying, "Wow!"

g_middle.title: The Big Cheer
paragraphs: You hold very still on Gus's shoulders. The crowd cheers. Hats fly up. Peanut barks. Dottie waves her arms.
Beep, beep! Recording saved.
"Bye, Dottie! Bye, Gus!" you call. You wave the paper sunflower. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch plays the cheer. It is loud and happy. "Evelyn, this is perfect," she says.
You put the paper sunflower on the fridge. Wait! Can it come home? Dr. Finch smiles. "It's paper, and it was a gift. I think it's okay."

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: On Pedestrian Day, people walked from both ends and met in the middle. The middle of the bridge is 4,200 feet from tower to tower. In 1937, that was the longest span of any suspension bridge in the world.

photos.caption: People walk across the Golden Gate Bridge on Pedestrian Day, May 27, 1937.
photos.credit: Still from a 1937 opening-day film, Prelinger Archives / Internet Archive (public domain)

photos.caption: The finished Golden Gate Bridge from the southwest, September 3, 1937.

g_wind.title: The Wind Song
paragraphs: You hold the rail. You hold still. You record the wind. Whoosh! You record the road creak, just a tiny bit.
Beep, beep! Recording saved. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch listens. "The bridge bends so it won't break," you say. "Like a tree."
"That's right," says Dr. Finch. "Good engineers plan for the wind."
Mom says, "Like my bees. They build strong, but not stiff."

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: The Golden Gate Bridge was built to move. In strong winds, the middle of the road can swing side to side. Moving a little keeps it safe.

photos.caption: The finished Golden Gate Bridge from the southwest, September 3, 1937.
The Golden Gate Bridge under construction, July 16, 1934.
photos.credit: Chas. M. Hiller / Library of Congress (no known restrictions)

g_fort.title: The Bridge Wakes Up
paragraphs: You hold still. You record the foghorns, and the waves, and the cheer far up high.
The band takes a picture, too. The fort, the arch, and the orange bridge, coming out of the fog.
Beep, beep! Recording saved. Zap! You are home.
"You waited for the fog to move," says Dr. Finch. "That was smart."
"I learned it on a ferry," you say.

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: Fort Point is a brick fort. It was built about the time of the Civil War. The bridge builders saved it. They built a steel arch so the bridge could pass right over it.

photos.caption: Fort Point, the old brick fort, with the new bridge going up over it, 1934.
photos.credit: Roger Sturtevant / Historic American Buildings Survey / Library of Congress

photos.caption: The finished Golden Gate Bridge from the southwest, September 3, 1937.

g_gus.title: Gus's Story
paragraphs: You hold up the band. "Tell it again, please," you say.
Gus tells all about the hard hats, the net, and the cables. Dottie adds, "And Evelyn found Peanut!" Peanut yips.
Beep, beep! Recording saved.
"Bye!" you call. Dottie waves. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch plays it at the museum. Now, every day, people hear a real worker tell how he built the bridge.

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: Workers on the bridge wore hard hats. A big safety net hung under them. The net caught 19 men who fell. Sadly, not everyone was saved. Eleven workers died building the bridge. People still remember their names.

photos.caption: A pylon on the San Francisco side, early in the work, 1934.
Early work on the bridge over Fort Point.
photos.credit: U.S. Army / U.S. National Park Service

g_strauss.title: The Mighty Task
paragraphs: You hold still. Mr. Strauss reads. The crowd claps. A band plays.
Beep, beep! Recording saved. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch plays it. "At last the mighty task is done."
"He didn't do it by himself," you say. "Lots of workers helped. And Mr. Ellis did the math. And Mr. Morrow drew the towers."
"That's right," says Dr. Finch. "Big things take lots of people."

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: Joseph Strauss was the chief engineer. On May 27, 1937, he read his poem at Crissy Field. Many people helped him. Charles Ellis did much of the math, and Irving Morrow designed how the bridge looks.

photos.caption: Joseph Strauss, the chief engineer. His is the big picture in the official program from the 1937 opening.
photos.credit: Official Souvenir Program, Golden Gate Bridge Fiesta, 1937. Prelinger Library / Internet Archive (not in copyright)

photos.caption: The finished Golden Gate Bridge from the southwest, September 3, 1937.

g_peanut.title: Yip, Yip, Hooray!
paragraphs: You hold still. Peanut yips. Dottie laughs. "Good boy, Peanut!" Gus laughs too, a big, deep laugh.
Beep, beep! Recording saved.
"Bye, Dottie!" you call. You hold your paper sunflower tight. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch plays it. Yip, yip! Mom laughs so hard, she has to sit down.
"You did not just record the day," says Dr. Finch. "You helped make it happy."

really_there.title: You were really there
really_there.text: On Pedestrian Day, people brought their pets. Some walked dogs across. One person even walked a cat on a leash! A newspaper said the first lost girl on the bridge was found, too.

photos.caption: People walk across the Golden Gate Bridge on Pedestrian Day, May 27, 1937.
photos.credit: Still from a 1937 opening-day film, Prelinger Archives / Internet Archive (public domain)

photos.caption: A huge crowd gathers at the Golden Gate Bridge on Pedestrian Day, May 27, 1937.
photos.credit: Still from a 1937 opening-day film, Prelinger Archives / Internet Archive (public domain)

e_stand_out.title: Everyone Stares
paragraphs: Zap! You land at the bridge in 1937. But you have on your sparkly sneakers and your shirt from today.
People stare. "What funny shoes!" says a lady. A policeman bends down. "Where is your mother, little girl?"
You don't want to change what happened. Beep! The band brings you home.
What could you try differently? Next time, try on the 1937 clothes first.

e_out_of_charges.title: Out of Dots
paragraphs: You tap the band. It goes blip. Then, nothing. All three dots are dark.
"Oh no," says Dr. Finch. "You used all your trips."
The band needs to charge all night. The bridge will have to wait.
What could you try differently? You only have three dots. Pick your trips with care.

e_safety_return.title: Safety Return
paragraphs: Beep, beep, beep! The band flashes red. Zap!
You are back in the kitchen. "The band brought you home," says Dr. Finch. "It does that if something is not safe. And it does that if you might change what happened."
She gives you a big hug. "You are safe. That's what matters most."
What could you try differently? Watch and be kind. Don't climb, jump, or touch the work.

e_time_up.title: Time's Up
paragraphs: Tick, tock. The band beeps. The clock says zero.
Zap! You are home. You did not record anything.
"Each trip only lasts one hour," says Dr. Finch. "Then the band brings you back."
What could you try differently? Watch the clock on the band. Don't wait too long.

e_cars_day.title: The Day for Cars
paragraphs: Zap! You land by the bridge. Honk, honk! Cars zoom past. No one is walking on the road.
It is May 28, the day after Pedestrian Day. At noon, President Roosevelt pressed a special key far away in Washington. That told everyone the bridge was open to cars.
It is fun to see. But there is no walk to record today. Beep! The band brings you home.
What could you try differently? Pedestrian Day was May 27.

e_too_loud.title: Too Loud!
paragraphs: BOOOOO! The horn is so loud and deep! You jump. You cover your ears.
The band falls off your wrist. Clunk! The recording stops.
You pick it up. Beep! The band brings you home.
"What was that sound?" you ask. "A foghorn," says Dr. Finch. "It is loud, but it is a helper."
What could you try differently? Learn about foghorns first. A ferry ride in 1933 might help.

e_crowd.title: Lost in the Crowd
paragraphs: You go this way. Coats. You go that way. Backs. You jump. All you see are hats.
The crowd is so big, you can't find a spot. You get squished. You feel very small.
Beep! The band brings you home.
"Big crowds are hard," says Dr. Finch. "A friend can help."
What could you try differently? Maybe help someone on the bridge. Then they can help you.

e_squeeze.title: Stuck at the Gate
paragraphs: You squeeze. You wiggle. "Hey, no pushing!" says a big boy.
The crowd gets tight. You get stuck between two grown-ups. You can't move.
Beep! The band brings you home. You are safe, but you missed the opening.
What could you try differently? Wait your turn. Being kind is the best way.

e_fog.title: Gray, Gray, Gray
paragraphs: You hold still. You record. Beep, beep! Recording saved. Zap! You are home.
Dr. Finch looks at it. Gray. Just gray fog. You can hear the waves. But you can't see the bridge at all.
"Fog likes to hide things," she says.
What could you try differently? Learn about fog first. A ferry ride in 1933 might help.

e_count.title: Too Many Wires
paragraphs: "I know!" you say. "There are wires in there! Let me count them."
One, two, three... You count and count. Ten, eleven, twelve...
But you don't know how many there are! The kids walk away. Beep! The band brings you home.
"There are over twenty-seven thousand," says Dr. Finch. "You can't count that in one hour!"
What could you try differently? Watch the workers make the cables in 1936.
